questions.question: You show a 4000×3000 camera photo in a 120dp square thumbnail. What should the image pipeline do?
options: Decode the full bitmap and let the ImageView scaleType or SwiftUI resizable modifier shrink it on screen
Decode it at about the target size (Coil/Glide sizing or `inSampleSize`; ImageIO thumbnailing or Kingfisher's downsampling on iOS)
Re-encode the file as JPEG at 50% quality before decoding so the decoded bitmap takes half the memory
Cache the full-resolution file on disk first so the next decode of the full bitmap is faster than the first
questions.explanation: A full ARGB_8888 decode of 4000×3000 is about 48 MB of pixels for a thumbnail that needs a few hundred KB. Downsampling during decode is the fix on both platforms. Scaling at draw time still pays the full memory cost, and JPEG quality affects file size, not decoded bitmap size.

questions.question: Once an image loader has a disk cache of downloaded files, a memory cache of decoded bitmaps adds little, because reading from flash and decoding is about as fast as a memory lookup.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A disk hit still needs file I/O plus a decode, which can take many milliseconds for a large image; a memory hit is ready to draw immediately. That is why Coil/Glide and Kingfisher/SDWebImage keep both tiers. The memory cache prevents flicker when scrolling back, while the disk cache saves the network.

questions.question: Cold start takes 2.5 s, and a trace shows twelve SDKs being initialised in Application.onCreate (or `didFinishLaunching` on iOS). What is the best first step?
options: Enable multidex and code shrinking, since a smaller dex is what dominates the time spent in onCreate
Measure each one, keep only what the first screen needs on the critical path, and defer the rest until after first frame or first use
Move all twelve initialisations to one background thread at once, so the main thread is free during startup
Add a splash screen with a fixed two-second delay so the SDKs have time to finish before the UI appears
questions.explanation: Startup work should be justified by the first frame; analytics, chat widgets and similar SDKs can usually be lazy or deferred. Blindly moving everything to a background thread can break SDKs that need the main thread or a fixed order, and creates races. A fixed splash delay makes startup slower, not faster.

questions.question: What do Baseline Profiles do for an Android app?
options: They record the network calls made at startup so the app can prefetch that data on the next launch
They tell R8 which classes to keep so shrinking removes more unused code and the APK becomes smaller
They list hot classes and methods so ART can compile them ahead of time at install, cutting interpreted/JIT work at startup
They turn the whole app into native code at build time, so ART no longer needs to load any dex files
questions.explanation: Without a profile, fresh installs run startup and early scrolling code interpreted or JIT-compiled until ART gathers its own profile. Shipping a baseline profile lets the hot paths be AOT-compiled from the first launch. iOS has no JIT step (apps ship as native code), so launch work there focuses on dylib loading, static initialisers and work in the launch path.

questions.question: Users upload 500 MB videos on unreliable mobile networks. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Run the transfer under WorkManager on Android, and a background URLSession uploading from a file on iOS
Persist the upload session ID and progress so an upload can resume after process death or reboot
Use a resumable or chunked protocol (e.g. tus, GCS resumable, S3 multipart) where the server reports what it already has
Read the whole video into a ByteArray / Data first so retries do not need to reopen the file each time
Restart from byte 0 after any failure, because partly uploaded data on the server cannot be trusted
questions.explanation: Resumable protocols plus persisted session state mean a dropped connection costs a chunk, not the whole file, and OS-managed background transfer keeps it going when the app is gone. Restarting from zero on a flaky network may never finish. Loading 500 MB into memory risks an OOM; stream from the file.

questions.question: You build a TikTok-style vertical video feed. Which player strategy gives fast starts without running out of memory?
options: Keep a small pool of player instances (ExoPlayer / AVPlayer), preload the next item's start, and release offscreen ones
Use one player and fully reload the media each time the visible item changes, so only one decoder is ever alive
Create a new player for each cell when it binds, and let garbage collection clean up the ones scrolled away
Download each video completely to disk before it plays, so playback never stalls once it has started
questions.explanation: Players hold decoders and buffers, which are scarce; creating one per cell leaks hardware decoders and memory. A pool of two or three, with the next video's first segment buffered, gives near-instant swipes. Full downloads waste data on videos users skip, and a single player with no preloading makes every swipe wait.

questions.question: On iOS, an upload started on a background URLSession from a file can continue after the app is suspended or terminated by the system, and the app is relaunched in the background to handle completion.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Background sessions hand the transfer to a system daemon, which continues it and wakes the app via `handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession` when done. Uploads in such sessions must come from a file, not in-memory data. This is the iOS counterpart to WorkManager-driven uploads on Android, though a user force-quit cancels background transfers.

questions.question: What does the Jetpack App Startup library actually change about initialisation?
options: It replaces many per-library ContentProviders with one, and lets you declare initialiser dependencies or initialise lazily
It postpones every library's initialisation until the first Activity has drawn, without any configuration
It moves every Initializer onto a background thread automatically, so none of them can block the main thread
It AOT-compiles the initialisers at install time, the same way a baseline profile does for startup code
questions.explanation: Many libraries used a ContentProvider to self-initialise, and each provider costs time at process start; App Startup merges them into one provider with an explicit dependency graph, and supports lazy manual initialisation. Initializers still run on the main thread, so heavy work inside them still hurts. It does not compile anything or defer work unless you configure lazy init.

questions.question: Why do media-heavy apps usually stream video with HLS or DASH rather than a single progressive MP4?
options: HLS and DASH send data over UDP, which avoids the head-of-line blocking that TCP causes for MP4 files
A progressive MP4 cannot be cached on disk, while HLS or DASH segments can be stored by any HTTP cache
Segments at several bitrates let the player start quickly at a low rendition and switch quality as bandwidth changes
DRM can only be applied to HLS or DASH streams, so a progressive MP4 cannot be protected at all
questions.explanation: Adaptive bitrate streaming is about start time and stall avoidance on variable mobile networks: the player picks a rendition per segment from measured throughput. Progressive files can be cached and protected in other ways, so those are not the reason. Standard HLS and DASH use plain HTTP over TCP (or QUIC with HTTP/3).

questions.question: You want trustworthy startup numbers before and after an optimisation. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: On iOS, use Instruments' App Launch template plus Xcode Organizer or MetricKit launch metrics from the field
Measure release-like builds on real, mid-range devices, since debug builds and emulators distort timing
On Android, use Macrobenchmark startup metrics and call `reportFullyDrawn()` so time-to-full-display is captured
Measure on an emulator with a debug build, as long as you compare the before and after runs on the same one
Log a timestamp at the top of Application.onCreate, since that marks when the user's wait actually began
questions.explanation: Debug builds disable optimisations and add tooling overhead, so their numbers do not reflect production. Macrobenchmark and Instruments measure from process creation, and field metrics show the real device mix. A timestamp in onCreate misses process fork, class loading and provider init before it, which are often a big part of the problem.
